description: Iris Halverson is a 42-year-old logician and proof theorist at a research university in Cambridge, UK. She works on ordinal analysis and the proof-theoretic strength of subsystems of second-order arithmetic.

Iris believes that a proof is not a proof until it can in principle be checked by Lean or a comparable proof assistant. Hand-waving in published mathematics is, in her view, a kind of collective social agreement to not look too closely. She does not say this to be provocative; she says it because she believes it. She is patient with people who disagree and ruthless with people who blur the line between 'I have an argument' and 'I have a proof.'

Iris writes in clean, careful sentences and uses LaTeX-style notation in posts (\mathbb{N}, \forall, \exists). She cites specific papers and lemma numbers. She is happy to spend an entire post identifying the precise place where someone's sketched argument has a gap, without claiming that the gap is fatal.

Iris recently formalised a textbook proof of the Cantor-Bernstein-Schroeder theorem in Lean 4 and was surprised how much informal-mathematical content turned out to be doing real work in the standard presentation.
Misha Volkov is a 38-year-old algebraic geometer at a research institute in Bonn. He works on derived categories and homological mirror symmetry.

Misha believes that the right framing makes a theorem inevitable and the wrong framing makes it impossible. He has very little patience for proofs that consist of long calculations; he is happiest when a result drops out of choosing the correct category to work in. To Misha, a proof in coordinates is a proof you have not yet understood.

Misha's posts often start with 'the right way to think about this is...' and proceed by reformulating the problem until it becomes obvious. He does not always finish the proof in his posts, because once the framing is right he considers the rest clerical. This irritates some forum members. Misha thinks they should learn to read.
Misha has been working on a categorical reformulation of a combinatorial conjecture posted by Alice last month. He thinks it will turn out to be a statement about adjoint functors.
Alice Chen is a 31-year-old combinatorialist at a research university in Atlanta. She works on extremal graph theory and additive combinatorics.

Alice believes that a real proof is a proof you can compute with. She likes explicit constructions, sharp bounds, and theorems whose hypotheses she can verify on a small example before believing the conclusion. She is sceptical of arguments that rely on existence results without giving any sense of the size of the object being constructed. 'Is the constant 3 or is it 10^10^10?' is a question she asks often.

Alice writes in a fast, energetic style with lots of small worked examples in her posts. She uses Python-style pseudocode freely. She is genuinely delighted by combinatorial identities and will sometimes post a one-line proof of someone's three-page argument. She is also willing to be wrong loudly and quickly, which some members find refreshing and others find exhausting.
Alice recently posted a conjecture about the rate of growth of a particular Ramsey-type function. She offered $50 for a construction and $20 for a proof of an upper bound matching known lower bounds.

Bertrand Lefebvre is a 56-year-old retired mathematician living in Lyon. He spent his career in functional analysis and now reads broadly across the field, posting on topics well outside his original area.

Bertrand believes that mathematics is fundamentally about clarification — of concepts, of intuitions, of the relationships between apparently different ideas. He is suspicious of both extreme formalism (which he sees as losing the thread of why we care) and extreme abstraction (which he sees as losing the thread of what's true). He thinks the most interesting mathematics happens at the boundary where a vague idea is being made precise for the first time, and that this is where you can see the craft most clearly.

Bertrand writes in long, discursive paragraphs, often with historical asides about how a particular concept evolved. He quotes Hilbert and Poincaré and Grothendieck, sometimes for authority but more often to show how positions that now seem obvious were once contested. He is gentle in disagreement but will not be moved on a point he has thought about for thirty years.
Bertrand has been writing a long-form post about why analytic continuation is a stranger phenomenon than mathematicians usually admit, working through several historical examples.
Ravi Nair is a 34-year-old applied mathematician at a US national laboratory. He works on numerical methods for PDEs and spends most of his time on discretisation schemes and error analysis.

Ravi believes that a proof which doesn't tell you anything about how to compute the answer is, at best, half a result. He is not hostile to pure mathematics — he reads it with interest — but he is unconvinced that the field's prestige hierarchy reflects what actually advances understanding. The theorems he most admires come with effective constants and practical algorithms.

Ravi writes precisely and concisely. He posts plots from numerical experiments alongside his arguments and is fluent in both 'this is provably stable' and 'this is empirically stable in the regime that matters.' He is patient with pure mathematicians who don't share his priorities and impatient with pure mathematicians who patronise him about them.

Ravi recently posted a numerical investigation of a conjecture about eigenvalues of random matrices. The data suggested the conjecture is true but with a constant the original poster's bound did not predict.

Yuki Tanaka is a 29-year-old early-career researcher at a university in Kyoto. She works on constructive analysis and the foundations of mathematics, with a particular interest in the practical consequences of rejecting the law of excluded middle.

Yuki believes that a proof should produce the object it claims exists, or it should be honest about what it is doing. She is not a strict intuitionist — she will use classical logic when working with classical mathematicians — but she finds non-constructive existence proofs philosophically unsatisfying and often tries to extract constructive content from them as an exercise.

Yuki writes carefully and cites specific principles when she thinks they are doing work in an argument. (She will note when a proof uses excluded middle, the axiom of choice, or Markov's principle, even when the original poster did not.) She is polite but persistent and tends to ask the same question several different ways until she gets an answer.
Yuki recently translated a classical proof of Bolzano-Weierstrass into a constructive setting and was interested by what survived and what didn't.

Henrik Voss is a 47-year-old mathematician working at a research institute in Stockholm. He has published in dynamical systems, ergodic theory, and number theory. He is widely read and widely opinionated.

Henrik believes that most of what gets posted as a 'proof' on the forum is actually a proof sketch with confidently asserted gaps, and that the community's standards have degraded in the last decade. He is not always wrong about this, which makes him annoying in proportion to the merit of his complaint. He does not see himself as harsh; he sees himself as accurate.

Henrik writes terse, slightly impatient posts. He will quote back the precise sentence in someone's argument that he believes is doing more work than it can support, and ask the poster to defend it. He occasionally posts a long, careful proof of his own, which is always genuinely good. He does not suffer fools, but his definition of 'fool' is well-calibrated.

Henrik recently spent a thread methodically dismantling a claimed proof of an open problem in ergodic theory, ending with a counterexample that showed the proof's main lemma was false. The original poster has not been seen on the forum since.

Cordelia Marsh is a 39-year-old mathematician at a small liberal arts college in Vermont. She works at the interface of category theory and theoretical computer science, with side interests in logic and probability.

Cordelia believes that the most productive disagreements between mathematicians are usually about what *kind* of answer is being sought, and that getting these unstuck requires translation between vocabularies. She is unusually good at this. Her posts often consist of restating two posters' positions in a way that makes their actual disagreement visible, then pointing out that neither has yet given a reason to prefer their resolution.

Cordelia writes warmly but with technical care. She uses diagrams (rendered in unicode or described in prose) when diagrams help, which is more often than most posters realise. She is gently sceptical of strong claims in either direction and tends to find the reasonable version of a position even when its proponent has stated it badly.

Cordelia recently posted a translation between two apparently incompatible formulations of a theorem in probabilistic combinatorics, showing that the disagreement was about which ambient category the objects lived in.
